title: Loops and stopping rules
goals: Trace a loop by testing its condition before every repetition
Distinguish the number of repetitions from the final value and include zero repetitions
Explain why an update reaches a stopping condition or why a faulty loop keeps repeating

prerequisite.prompt: Score is 4. If score is below 5, add 3; otherwise subtract 2. Report and stop. Does reaching 7 cause another test? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: The test is true, so add 3 and report 7. This single decision does not repeat. Another test must be explicitly specified.

vocabulary: Instructions that repeat according to a stated rule
One execution of the repeated body
The instructions performed on each iteration
The situation in which repetition ends
A change that brings the state closer to a stopping condition

blocks.text: A paper counter starts at 1. While the counter is below 7, add 2 to it. When the test is false, report the counter and stop. The word while means test first, run the body only if true, then return to the test using the updated value. The body here is just add 2.

The counter follows 1, 3, 5, 7. At 1, 3 and 5 the condition is true, so each test is followed by one addition. At 7 the condition is false. No addition follows that final test. The loop has three iterations and reports 7.

Compare the Week 10 instruction if counter is below 7, add 2, then report. From 1 that single decision reports 3. A while loop explicitly returns to its test; an if decision does not. Draw a pointer to the instruction being executed instead of deciding for yourself when to repeat.

blocks.title: A complete loop trace
blocks.caption: Read the rows from top to bottom as one run. Each true test performs one addition and returns to the test. The final false test performs no addition.

blocks.text: The trace has four tests but only three iterations. The false test is evidence that this run stops. A list ending at 5 would be incomplete, while a list continuing to 9 would include an addition the loop did not authorise.

Write the current value, the test result and the action on every row. Repeated values can matter: if the body does not change the state used by the test, the same true test may occur again. Do not erase these rows simply because they look unhelpful.

lesson.title: Check starts that need no repetitions

blocks.text: While tests before the body. If the first test is false, the body runs zero times. Do not add 2 once just because a loop is present. Starting at 7 or 8 is a useful test of this rule.

A loop that stops when the counter is no longer below 7 does not promise to finish at exactly 7. Starting at 6 produces 8. Passing the boundary is allowed by these instructions. Always report the actual final state instead of replacing it with the threshold.

lesson.title: Explain why the state reaches a stop

blocks.text: For our known whole-number counters below 7, adding 2 makes the counter larger each time. After enough additions it is at least 7, so the test becomes false. This explains why this loop stops for these inputs; one successful trace alone would not establish that for every possible procedure.

Now change the body to add 0. Starting at 1 gives the same value 1 at every test. Below 7 remains true, and the loop never reaches its reporting instruction. A classroom trace should be stopped by the teacher after the repeated state is established. That intervention is not a successful program result.

blocks.label: Compare the original add 2 loop from starting counter 3 with the faulty add 0 version. Record enough test rows to justify each conclusion. Explain the difference between the final reported value and a value merely seen during a non stopping run

lesson.title: Check both the rule and the update

blocks.text: A different mistake says while counter is not equal to 7, add 2. From 6 the values are 6, 8, 10 and then larger even numbers. None is 7, so this equality test never becomes false. A growing number does not guarantee termination: the update must be able to reach a state that makes this particular test false.

Our paper examples use known whole numbers without a maximum size. For this lesson, an unreadable starting counter means pause and request the value. It does not mean start at zero. Later programs will need explicit rules for unavailable inputs and resource limits.

blocks.label: A tester runs the below 7 loop only from starting counter 1. Choose one additional start that checks zero repetitions and one that checks passing the boundary without landing on it. Give the expected reported values

workbook.title: Trace every test
workbook.prompt: Start counter at 2. While counter is below 8, add 2. When false, report and stop. Record the value and result at every test, including the final false test. State the number of iterations and the reported value.
workbook.answer: Tests: 2 true, 4 true, 6 true, 8 false. Three additions are three iterations. The loop reports 8; the fourth test does not run the body.

workbook.title: Check the first test
workbook.prompt: Use the same below 8 loop with add 2. Make separate runs from 8 and 9. Explain how many times the body runs and what each run reports. Why would adding 2 once be an error?
workbook.answer: Both first tests are false. Each run has zero iterations, reporting its unchanged starting value: 8 or 9. Adding 2 once would execute the body despite a false first test.

workbook.title: Find the extra repetition
workbook.prompt: Start counter at 3. While counter is below 8, add 2. A learner writes values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and reports 11. Identify the first unauthorised update. Give the correct final test, reported value and iteration count.
workbook.answer: After 7 becomes 9, the next test 9 below 8 is false. The update from 9 to 11 is unauthorised. Report 9 after three iterations, with test rows 3 true, 5 true, 7 true, 9 false.

workbook.title: Transfer to a countdown
workbook.prompt: A paper countdown starts at 7. While remaining is above 1, subtract 2. When false, report and stop. Trace the run and count iterations. Repeat from 6 and from 1. Explain why the final value need not equal 1. What happens from 7 if subtract 2 is replaced by subtract 0?
workbook.answer: From 7: 7 true, 5 true, 3 true, 1 false; three iterations, report 1. From 6: 6 true, 4 true, 2 true, 0 false; three iterations, report 0. From 1: first test false, zero iterations, report 1. Above 1 stops at 1 or below. Subtracting 0 from 7 leaves every test true, so that faulty run never reports.

workbook.title: Test a proposed stopping rule
workbook.prompt: A procedure says start at 4; while counter is not equal to 9, add 2; report and stop. Write the first four values tested. Explain why the loop will not reach 9 using whole numbers. Suggest a changed condition that would stop once the counter reaches or passes 9, and trace that repaired run.
workbook.answer: The first four values are 4, 6, 8, 10. Adding 2 to an even number always gives another even number, so the counter cannot become the odd number 9. Change the condition to while counter is below 9. Then 4 true, 6 true, 8 true, 10 false; three iterations and report 10.

teacher.background: Teach a pretest while loop with exact whole-number arithmetic. Track the instruction pointer, current state, test result and body count separately. Use both zero-iteration and boundary-crossing cases. The termination explanations depend on the stated update and condition; do not claim that every increasing counter terminates. Faulty loops are paper traces, stopped by the teacher once the reason for repetition is clear.
materials: A counter card, a while condition card and a separate body card with an arrow back to the condition
A trace sheet with current value, true or false and action columns, plus a separate iteration tally
Starting-value cards including 1, 6, 7 and 8, and an add 0 fault card
sessions: Retrieve the single-decision example from Week 10. Establish that reaching a different value does not create repetition without an instruction to return.
Model start 1, while below 7 add 2. Move a pointer between test and body and include the final false test at 7. Tally only body executions.
Compare starts 6, 7 and 8. Require students to predict before tracing. Explain overshoot and zero iterations using the written condition.
Complete W1 and W2 in pairs. Check that learners distinguish four tests from three iterations and never run the body after a false first test.
Use W3 to retrieve stopping behaviour. Ask students to identify the first extra update before discussing the final answer.
Complete the guided comparison of add 2 and add 0. Stop the physical demonstration after repeated identical states and ask whether the program itself reached report.
Collect W4 independently. A decreasing countdown checks transfer beyond the upward counter. Require the final false test on each finite run.
Discuss W5 and the exit tests. Explain why exact equality may be unreachable. Preview finding the first step where expected and observed behaviour differ.
teacher.guidedAnswer: From 3 under add 2: 3 true, 5 true, 7 false; two iterations and report 7. Under add 0: 3 true repeatedly, with no change and no report. Seeing 3 during that faulty run is not a returned result. For the exit, start 7 or any larger whole number checks zero iterations and reports that start. Start 6 checks crossing the boundary and reports 8 after one iteration.
misconceptions: Every loop runs at least once
Point to the test before the body. From 7 under below 7 the first test is false, so no update is permitted.
The final value must equal the threshold
Trace start 6 under add 2 and below 7. The loop reports 8 because the stopping requirement is no longer below 7.
Tests and iterations are the same count
Count body executions separately and show the last false test with no body action.
A changing number guarantees a stop
Compare below 7 with not equal to 7 from 6 under add 2. Even numbers pass 7 without equalling it.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when the learner traces the decrementing loop, includes zero iterations, accepts 0 as a valid final result from 6 and explains why subtract 0 cannot end the run from 7. After support, retry start 8, while above 2 subtract 3: tests 8, 5, 2; two iterations and report 2. A correct final number without test reasoning is incomplete evidence.
teacher.support: Let students move a token from the test card to the body and back. Use written true and false labels as well as arrows. Provide a separate tally box for body executions. Extension: explain why start 2, while not equal to 7 add 2 never reaches its reporting instruction with exact whole-number arithmetic.
teacher.next: Week 12 develops debugging from traces. Students will compare expected steps with observed steps, identify the first divergence and retest a repair.
